Mario Party 4 PowerPC Edition
=============================
Version 0.9.20


WHAT THIS IS

A native PowerPC port of Mario Party 4, built from the mariopartyrd
decompilation and running as a real Mac OS X application on a Power Mac G4.
This is not an emulator: the game's own C code is compiled for the G4's
processor, its 99 code modules load as native bundles, and the GameCube's
GX graphics commands are translated into OpenGL 1.3 for the Radeon 9000
as the game produces them, with the transform and lighting on the card's
vertex unit and the audio mixed on the CPU.  A board plays at the console's
speed with the picture at 30 frames a second.

Drag the application into your Applications folder.


WHAT IT NEEDS

The game checks the machine every time it starts, before the window opens,
and says what it found in the window's title and on the log.

Minimum: a PowerPC G4 Mac running Mac OS X 10.4 or later, 256 MB of
memory, and a graphics card of the Radeon 9000 class or better -- four or
more texture units with ATI's combiner extensions -- on which the game
runs, slower than a console on anything under 800 MHz.

Recommended: a dual 1 GHz G4 (or better) with a 64 MB Radeon 9000 or
better and Mac OS X 10.5.  That is the machine the port was built on, where
it runs at console speed.

By card, as far as the drivers' extension lists say (only the first line
has been run on real hardware):

    ATI Radeon 9000 / 9000 Pro, 64 MB         runs at full speed (the
    (Power Mac G4 2002-03)                    reference card)
    ATI Radeon 9000 / 9200 / Mobility 9200,   runs; the texture cache is
    32 MB (eMac 2004, iBook G4, PowerBook     sized down to the card, and
    12"/15" 2003)                             a first run says so
    ATI Radeon 9600 / 9700 / 9800 and their   expected to run at full
    Mobility versions (PowerBook G4 2004+,    speed; not yet tried
    Power Mac G4 / G5)
    NVIDIA GeForce FX 5200 / 6600             unknown: it depends on whether
                                              Apple's driver lists the ATI
                                              combiner extension
    NVIDIA GeForce4 MX / GeForce2 MX,         refused: two or three texture
    ATI Radeon 7500 / 7000 / Rage 128         units cannot draw the picture

A machine below the minimum gets a dialog saying why, and the game does not
start.  A machine that runs but below what the port was built for gets that
dialog once, then runs.  An Intel Mac is refused: the PowerPC binary does run
under Rosetta, but slowly and with a different picture, and it is not what
this is built for.

SDL2 is inside the application; there is nothing else to install.


YOU BRING THE DISC IMAGE

No game data is included.  You need your own dump of your Mario Party 4 disc
-- the USA release, revision 1 (game id GMPE01) -- as a .iso; a trimmed NKit
.iso is fine, and so is a folder holding the disc's extracted files/ tree.

The first time you open the game it asks for that file with a standard Open
dialog, checks that it is the right disc, and remembers where it is.  You are
not asked again.  If you move the image the game asks once more; to point it
at a different image, move the old one out of the way or delete the `image`
line from the config file (see WHERE YOUR THINGS LIVE).

Two ways to skip the dialog altogether: put the .iso in a folder named
MarioParty4 in your home folder (~/MarioParty4/), where the game looks
before asking; or run it from the Terminal with --image and the path.


THE SCREEN

A first run comes up fullscreen: the 640x480 picture scaled to the largest
4:3 rectangle that fits your display, letterboxed black at the sides, and the
choice is remembered.  For a window instead, run it once from the Terminal
(with the application in your Applications folder):

    "/Applications/Mario Party 4.app/Contents/MacOS/isle" --windowed

or change `fullscreen = 1` to `fullscreen = 0` in the config file.  Either is
remembered from then on; --fullscreen puts it back.


THE WATER

The GameCube ripples some of its water with a trick the Radeon's fixed
pipeline cannot do per pixel (a second texture bending the first one's
picture).  Since 0.9.13 the port does it at the corners of the water's
triangles instead, from the game's own ripple texture, so the water moves
with the game's own waves -- close to the console where the water is a fine
grid (Makin' Waves), fainter where the console bends it by a copy of the
picture itself, which the port cannot read back cheaply (Mario Medley's
second ripple, Cheep Cheep Sweep's reflection).  Three levels:

    off       flat water, as before 0.9.13
    cheap     the ripple at the water's own corners (costs almost nothing)
    full      each water triangle split into four first: smoother, and
              meant for a faster Mac than the reference machine
    auto      (the default) full on a faster Mac, off on a slower one, and
              on the reference machine the level each minigame measured
              room for: cheap in most, full in one, off in the rafts' river

Run once from the Terminal with --water off (or cheap, full, auto), or put
`water = cheap` in the config file; the choice is remembered.

Since 0.9.14 the water has this port's own look, tuned by eye on the G4
rather than copied from the console:

    Makin' Waves        the waves two and a half times the console's and
                        no sky reflected in the pool
    Cheep Cheep Sweep   the pond reads as deep water: the floor darkened
                        and blued under it, and the sky and the trees on
                        the water ("sky", the default), or the same water
                        with no sky ("tint")
    Mario Medley        the pool's blue now matches the console's

The console's own amplitude and sky come back with --waterlook console
(`waterlook = console` in the config file); the pond's choice is
--pondlook sky or --pondlook tint (`pondlook = tint`); --wavegain PERCENT
sets the waves on every rippling pool (100 is the console's).  All of them
are remembered like the water level.


LITE MODE

Seven minigames draw more than the reference machine (a dual 1 GHz G4
with a Radeon 9000) can finish in a thirtieth of a second, however the
drawing is done.  Since 0.9.17 those seven draw a little less there, and
since 0.9.19 all seven reach 30 frames a second: this is Lite mode.  What changes is only what is
drawn -- never what the game does.  The characters move, score, collide
and are dealt their luck exactly as with Lite off; the port checks that
frame by frame (the game's random numbers, every model's position and the
players' records are the same with Lite on and off).

What Lite changes, by default ("auto") on the reference machine:

    Butterfly Blitz        no shadows under the butterflies and the
                           nets; every other big flower by the fence
                           left out
    Manta Rings            the lighter character models
    Fruits of Doom         the lighter character models
    Darts of Doom          the lighter character models
    Order Up               the lighter character models
    Reversal of Fortune    the lighter character models
    Panel Panic            the lighter character models

"The lighter character models" are the game's own: every character comes
on the disc in three versions of decreasing detail, and the game already
uses the lighter ones in its busier minigames (Manta Rings and Panel Panic
use the middle one).  Lite takes the next one down -- the same character,
the same animations, fewer polygons.  Side by side the difference is in
the hands, the hair and the rounder parts of the face.

The round shadow (0.9.19, m441.blob below) is the one you may remember
from the Nintendo 64: a soft dark disc on the ground under each net, drawn
by the port in a few triangles instead of the net's real shadow, which
costs a whole extra drawing of every net each frame.  It follows the net
and fades a little as the net rises; the game never sees it.  It is not
in the default set: on the reference machine Butterfly Blitz read 30.0,
29.9 and 29.9 frames a second with it against 30.0 without it (no dearer
to draw, but the rule for the default set was 30.0 every time).  To have
it, put

    liteopts = ref,m441.blob

in the config file.

Since 0.9.20 there is also the whole idea (m441.bloball): every shadow in
Butterfly Blitz a round blob -- under each character, net, basket and
butterfly -- so the shadows are easy to see and the game's shadow pass has
nothing left to draw.  It is cheaper than the shadows it replaces (the
reference machine's drawn frame 20.2 ms against 24.1 with the default set;
30.0 frames a second in three runs out of three) and, like every Lite
option, changes nothing the game does.  It is off until you choose it --
the picture is docs/screenshots/m51-blob-all-m441.jpg in the project, the
console's shadows, today's Lite and the blobs side by side.  To have it:

    liteopts = ref,m441.bloball

Every other screen is drawn exactly as before.  A faster Mac than the
reference gets no Lite at all.  A slower one gets the same set and a few
extras on top, which the reference machine does not need: fewer fish and
no drifting bubbles in Manta Rings, and no shadows under the fruit stands
and the side pillars in Bowser's arena (Fruits of Doom, Darts of Doom).

Butterfly Blitz keeps its own character models since 0.9.18: the game
works out where each net is -- and so which butterflies are caught --
from a joint of the character's hand, and in the lighter models that
joint sits a little elsewhere (for Donkey Kong a good way off).  With
the lighter models the game would play differently, so Lite leaves them
out there.  (m441.char below still turns them on, for anyone who prefers
the speed -- knowing the catches can then differ from the console's.)

To turn it off -- the console's drawing everywhere, the seven slower --
run the game once from the Terminal with --nolite, or put

    lite = off

in the config file (WHERE YOUR THINGS LIVE).  --lite (lite = on) turns
the same set on whatever the Mac; --liteauto (lite = auto) is the
default.  All three are
remembered.  The options can also be picked one by one with --liteopts
and their names (liteopts = ... in the config file):

    m441.char      Butterfly Blitz: the lighter character models (not
                   in the default set: changes the catches)
    m441.bshadow   Butterfly Blitz: the butterflies cast no shadow
    m441.nshadow   Butterfly Blitz: the nets and baskets cast no shadow
    m441.blob      Butterfly Blitz: a round shadow under each net instead
                   (with or without m441.nshadow, the nets' own shadows go)
    m441.bloball   Butterfly Blitz: every shadow a round blob (the
                   characters, nets, baskets and butterflies)
    m441.rings     Butterfly Blitz: every other big flower by the fence
    m401.char      Manta Rings: the lighter character models
    m401.fish      Manta Rings: each fish school drawn to 10 fish
    m401.bubbles   Manta Rings: the drifting bubbles not drawn
    m436.char      Fruits of Doom: the lighter character models
    m436.plates    Fruits of Doom: the plates cast no shadow
    m436.pillars   Fruits of Doom: the two side pillars cast no shadow
    m435.char      Darts of Doom: the lighter character models
    m435.pillars   Darts of Doom: the two side pillars cast no shadow
    m431.char      Order Up: the lighter character models
    m444.char      Reversal of Fortune: the lighter character models
    m463.char      Panel Panic: the lighter character models

(ref is the default set, extras the slower Macs' additions -- m401.fish,
m401.bubbles, m436.plates, m436.pillars, m435.pillars -- and all is every
one.)  0.9.17 also draws Order Up's
sparkles faster with the same pixels, for everyone.  0.9.18 fixes the
lighter models' eyes in Fruits of Doom and Darts of Doom: when Bowser
chars the loser, the eyes stay white, as on the console.


BENCHMARK MODE

Mario Party 4 can measure your Mac and choose its settings itself.  Press
F1 (on a laptop keyboard fn-F1) or M at any time in the game: a small menu
opens over the picture.  The arrow keys or the controller's stick choose,
Return or A selects, Esc or B goes back; F1 or M again closes it.  While
the menu is open the game goes on underneath but your controllers do
nothing in it.  The very first time the game starts it offers Benchmark
Mode by itself, once.

"Run Benchmark Mode" closes the game and plays five scenes by itself, each
in its own window, for about five minutes (a few more when a scene lands
right at the line and is played three times, as the port's own speed
tests do; twice that on a slow Mac):

    1. the opening movie
    2. Toad's Midway Madness, a board with four computer players
    3. Butterfly Blitz, the heaviest minigame, with Lite off
    4. Butterfly Blitz again with Lite on -- only if it needed it
    5. Makin' Waves, the heaviest water

Each is the same short trip the port's own speed tests make (the computer
players walk in from the start, the game hurries undrawn to the scene, and
the scene is timed as it plays at real speed).  Please don't touch the
controls while it runs.  Your memory card is never touched -- the scenes
play on a scratch card.  Then the game opens again and shows, in plain
words, how fast this Mac is next to the reference machine (a dual 1 GHz
Power Mac G4 with a Radeon 9000), the frame rate of each scene, and what
it chose:

    Lite mode   off on a faster Mac; on for the heaviest screens (the
                default set) on one as fast as the reference; the default
                set and the extras on a slower one (LITE MODE)
    Water       the ripples where the Mac keeps up, flat where it does not
                (THE WATER)
    Movies      on when the opening movie plays at full speed (MOVIES)
    Memory      the memory kept for loading, by the memory installed
                (LOADING)

These go into the config file (WHERE YOUR THINGS LIVE) as lite, liteopts,
water, movies and resident -- the same lines the PowerPCube launcher uses
-- and stay until you change them or run Benchmark Mode again.

It also leaves a report on your Desktop, MarioParty4-benchmark-DATE.txt:
the Mac's model, processors and speed, memory, graphics card and its
memory, the system version and the game's version, each scene's frame rate
(with Lite off and on), and the settings chosen.  Nothing personal -- no
names, no file paths of yours -- so it can be sent to anyone helping you.
The scenes' own logs are in the Benchmark folder next to the config.

On the reference machine Benchmark Mode chooses what the game already
does by default (Lite at auto, the water at auto, the movies on, 256 MB
kept), so running it there changes nothing.


DEVELOPER MODE

The tools the game was tested with, for anyone playtesting it: open the
menu (F1 or M) and choose Developer Mode.

  Minigame marathon
    Plays every minigame one after another -- or a range of them (From /
    To), or one kind (4-player, 1-vs-3, 2-vs-2, Battle, the rest), or your
    own list (the minigame numbers, 401 to 463, in a file named
    marathon-list.txt next to the config).  Choose how many of you play
    (1 to 4; the computer plays the rest) and who plays whom, then Start.
    The game closes and opens again for each minigame: it hurries there by
    itself (about a minute on a 1 GHz G4: the board is played
    undrawn by four computer players and the roulette is set to the
    minigame), stops at the minigame's instruction card for you -- press
    START when you are ready (Z for the practice round) -- and after its
    results the next one loads.  Your
    memory card is not touched.  F1 or M during a minigame offers "Stop
    the marathon here"; closing the window stops it too.  Either way the
    results so far are kept, and Developer Mode offers "Resume the stopped
    marathon".  At the end (or at a stop) the game opens with a summary:
    every minigame played, the coins each player won in it, who won most.
    The summary is also saved in Documents/MarioParty4 Recordings.
    "Record each minigame" records every one of them (below).

  Record this session
    Turn it on and every launch of the game is recorded from the start:
    the four controllers, every frame, and what the game started from (its
    clock, the memory card as it was, the settings).  A recording starts
    at the boot, so turning it on offers "Restart now and record".  It
    stays on until you turn it off here (the recording in progress is
    closed and kept).  Recordings go to Documents/MarioParty4 Recordings,
    named by the date and time (a few megabytes an hour), with a copy of
    the memory card beside each one.  Recording costs nothing you can see:
    Butterfly Blitz and a board both played at 30.0 frames a second, three
    times each, with it on and off.

    What a recording is for: played back on the Mac (the G4 video below)
    it is the same game frame for frame, and turned into a Dolphin movie it
    plays in Dolphin (WATCHING A RECORDING IN DOLPHIN).

  Soak planner
    For the developers: the game playing itself for hours with four
    computer players, logging every fault, stall and frame rate.  Choose
    the board (or every board in turn), the turns, the minigames (the
    roulette's, or the marathon's choice), Lite, the water, snapshots and
    the length, and start it -- or only save the plan, soak-plan.txt next
    to the config, which the lab's tools read too (isle --soakplan FILE
    plays it from the Terminal).


WATCHING A RECORDING IN DOLPHIN

A session recording (.rec) becomes a Dolphin input movie (.dtm) on a
computer that has Dolphin: port/tools/rec2dtm.py and
port/tools/dolphin_sync.py (in the project's source) run Dolphin a number
of times to find, for every frame you played, the moment the console
reaches it -- the console waits on its disc where the Mac does not -- and
write session.dtm and GMPE01.ini.  To watch it on a Mac:

  1. Dolphin 2506 or later (dolphin-emu.org), and your own disc image of
     Mario Party 4 (USA, Rev 1, GMPE01).
  2. Copy GMPE01.ini into Dolphin's GameSettings folder
     (~/Library/Application Support/Dolphin/GameSettings/GMPE01.ini; if
     one is there already, add its [Gecko] and [Gecko_Enabled] lines to
     yours), and turn on Config > General > Enable Cheats.  The code it
     holds hands the game the board's random seeds the Mac used (the
     console takes them from its clock, which no movie can set).
  3. Use session-mac.dtm (it asks Dolphin for the Vulkan renderer; the
     movie sets the emulation settings that matter by itself: one CPU
     thread, the JIT, the DSP's HLE, the console's disc speed, English).
     Config > GameCube: "Skip Main Menu" on (the console's boot animation
     would put every frame late), and leave "Enable Custom RTC" off -- the
     movie carries the date and time the recording started from.
  4. The memory card: a recording made on a fresh card needs nothing (the
     movie asks Dolphin for a new, empty card and leaves yours alone).  A
     recording made on your own card comes with NAME.rec.card.raw: put it
     in Slot A (Config > GameCube > Slot A: Memory Card, the folder icon)
     for the replay, and put your own card back after.
  5. Movie > Play Input Recording... > session-mac.dtm, and choose the
     disc image.  Leave Movie > Read-Only Mode on.

Dolphin then plays the session by itself.  Lite mode does not matter:
the console has none, and Lite never changes what the game does, so a
session played with Lite on replays the same game in Dolphin.


MAKING A VIDEO OF A RECORDING

For the developers (the tools are in the project's source, port/tools, and
expect the lab's setup: a Linux machine with ffmpeg that reaches the G4 over
ssh, and Dolphin for the second half):

    port/tools/session_video.sh NAME.rec [--from FRAME] [--to FRAME]

plays the recording again on the G4 at the game's own pace frame by frame
(nothing dropped, every frame drawn and saved, the sound mixed exactly as it
was heard), and makes NAME-g4.mp4; then, once tools/dolphin_sync.py has
found the console's timeline for it, NAME-side.mp4: the G4 on the left,
Dolphin on the right, in step, with the G4's sound.  FRAME counts the
game's frames from the boot (the recording's own numbering).


LOADING

Loading a minigame or a board is a read of your disc image, and on a slow
or busy disk that read can hold the game for half a second or more (the
picture and the music pause together; the game then catches up).  Two things
in this version make those reads come from memory instead.  Neither changes
what the game does or when: the game reads the same bytes at the same
moment, and only where they come from is different.

    The read-ahead.  The moment the roulette stops on a minigame -- several
    seconds before the game loads it -- the module and its data are read
    into the system's file cache in the background, so the game's own read
    finds them there.  The same for the board at the results screen and for
    the board set at the mode select.  On a two-processor Mac this runs on
    the second processor; on a single processor it runs in small pieces in
    the idle time between frames, and not at all when there is none.  It is
    on for every machine; --noprefetch turns it off.

    The resident set.  The files every game reads -- the board's data, the
    instruction and results screens', the four characters' models and the
    sound banks -- are read once and kept in the game's own memory, and
    answered from there for the rest of the run; a minigame's files join
    the set as they are read ahead and the least recently used leave when
    it is full.  Its size is decided by the machine check from the memory
    installed: none under 768 MB, 128 MB with 1 GB, 256 MB with 1.5 GB or
    more, and never so much that the system and the game have less than
    about 600 MB between them.  --resident 0 turns it off; --resident 64
    (any number of megabytes) sets it by hand.  Both decisions are on the
    log's "machine:" lines and in --defaults.

Both can be set in the config file too (see WHERE YOUR THINGS LIVE), which
is where the PowerPCube launcher keeps them:

    prefetch = 0          no read-ahead (1, the default: on)
    resident = 128        the resident set's size: auto (the machine
                          check's choice, the default), 0, 64, 128 or 256

The game reads these lines at every start; only Benchmark Mode writes
one of them (resident, with the movies line, the water and Lite: see
BENCHMARK MODE).  A switch on the command line (--noprefetch or
--prefetch, --resident N or --resident auto) wins for the run it is given
to.

On the machine this was built on -- a dual 1 GHz Power Mac with 1.5 GB --
the two together turn a twenty-turn board's 319 MB of disc reading into
about 110 MB held in memory and one read from the disk, and a cold walk
through six minigames goes from thirty-odd reads over a tenth of a second
(three of them long enough to drop a second of game time) to three or
four.  The game uses about 110 MB more memory with the set than without.

Nothing is copied anywhere: the set is built from your own disc image at
every start and is gone when the game quits.


MOVIES

The game's movies play: the opening, the two short ones at the mode
select, the eight story-mode endings and the staff credits, with their
sound.  They are the disc's own files, decoded as the game plays them --
nothing is converted or stored anywhere -- by the game's own movie player
with a small decoder in the port standing in for the console's.  START or
A skips the opening, as on the console.

A movie is 608x448 at 30 frames a second, and a frame takes the reference
machine's second processor about 15 ms to decode.  The movie always runs
at its own speed, locked to its sound: on a machine that cannot keep up,
the picture shows fewer of the movie's frames -- a late frame is left out,
never waited for -- while the sound, the subtitles and the game around the
movie carry on exactly on time.  On the dual 1 GHz reference machine the
opening shows about 29 of its 30 frames a second, the two mode-select
movies (which play behind the menu's own 3D) 23 to 28.  On one processor
the same G4 shows about 29 and 23 to 26, and the sound does not break up
during any of them.

--nomovies skips every movie, as versions before 0.9.7 did.  The config
file's `movies = 0' does the same for every run (the PowerPCube launcher's
Movies switch writes it); --movies plays them for one run anyway.


CONTROLS

Keyboard (always active, beside a pad too)

    Arrow keys / WASD       control stick
    I K J L                 C stick
    T G F H                 D-pad up / down / left / right
    Z  X  C  V              A  B  X  Y
    Q  E                    L  R
    Shift or Tab            Z
    Return                  Start (the game's own pause, in a minigame)
    F5 (or F12)             screenshot onto the Desktop, as a PNG named by
                            the frame (Mac OS X 10.5 gives F12 to Dashboard
                            unless you change that in System Preferences)
    F1 or M                 the port's menu: Benchmark Mode, the settings
                            now (BENCHMARK MODE); Esc closes it
    Esc                     quit (closes the menu when it is open)
    Cmd+Q                   quit

Game pads: Xbox One controllers over USB are driven directly (no driver
to install); any other pad SDL recognises works through its own mapping.
Every pad plugged in before the game starts gets a port, in order: the
Xbox One pads first, then the others, up to four.  With one pad the
keyboard works beside it as player 1; to make the keyboard a controller
of its own -- player 2 on the keys, say -- run once from the Terminal:

    "/Applications/Mario Party 4.app/Contents/MacOS/isle" --kbport 2

(A port that has a controller makes that player human on the character
select, as on a console; players without one are computer players.  The
switch is not remembered: it is for the run it is given to.)

    Left stick              control stick
    Right stick             C stick
    A B X Y                 A B X Y
    LT / RT                 L / R (analogue, with the click near the end)
    LB                      Z
    Menu (Start)            Start
    D-pad                   D-pad

Rumble works on a pad that has it.

Changing the buttons.  The PowerPCube launcher's controls page writes a
plain text file the game reads at start (with no file, everything above is
exactly as it is):

    ~/Library/Application Support/PowerPCube/controls/mp4.txt

    player1 = keyboard        who plays on each port: auto (the order
    player2 = pad:1           above), keyboard, pad:N (the Nth pad in that
    player3 = none            order, 1 = the first) or none (a computer
                              player); this replaces --kbport
    key.a = Space             keys, by their SDL names, comma-separated
    key.start = Return,P
    pad.z = rightshoulder     pad buttons and axes, by SDL's names: a b x
    pad.a = a,righty-         y back start leftshoulder rightshoulder dpup
                              dpdown dpleft dpright, and the axes leftx
                              lefty rightx righty lefttrigger righttrigger
                              (with + or - for one direction: righty- is
                              the right stick pushed up)
    pad.stick = left          which stick is the control stick (left, right
    pad.cstick = right        or none), and the C stick

The names of the buttons are a b x y z l r start dup ddown dleft dright,
and for keys also stick_up stick_down stick_left stick_right and
cstick_up ... cstick_right.  A line not in the file keeps the mapping
above.  L and R stay analogue on a pad's triggers.  PowerPCube's pad
set-up also writes ~/Library/Application Support/PowerPCube/
gamecontrollerdb.txt, SDL mappings for pads SDL does not know; the game
loads it when it is there.  The log's "controls:" lines show the table the
game settled on.
Quitting -- Esc, Cmd-Q or the window's close button -- goes through the
game's own reset, as the console's Reset button does: the game fades, the
memory card is written, and the application leaves.  There is no separate
pause outside the game's own (Start, in a minigame).

For a bug report, the same line with --defaults prints every setting the
game would run with, and --keys the table above.  (Mac OS X 10.6's
open -a "Mario Party 4" --args ... does the same; the open of 10.4 and
10.5 has no --args.)  The log of the last run is in the folder below.


WHERE YOUR THINGS LIVE

    ~/Library/Application Support/MarioParty4/
        memcard-slot-a.raw    the memory card (a 59-block card image, the
                              same layout Dolphin uses, so a save moves
                              either way)
        config                the disc image's path, the fullscreen and
                              water choices (level, look, the pond), Lite,
                              and movies / prefetch / resident if set;
                              Benchmark Mode's choices
        benchmark-result.txt  Benchmark Mode's last result (and its
        benchmark/            scenes' logs)
        MarioParty4.log       the log of the last run
        marathon.txt          Developer Mode's marathon: the minigames, who
        marathon-result.txt   plays, the results so far; its last summary;
        marathon-logs/        each minigame's log
        marathon-list.txt     (yours, if you write it) a marathon's own list
        soak-plan.txt         the soak planner's plan

    ~/Documents/MarioParty4 Recordings/
        DATE TIME.rec         a session recording (Record this session),
        DATE TIME.rec.card.raw   with the memory card as it was at the start
        Marathon DATE.txt     each marathon's summary

Deleting the folder loses your save file, so that is the folder to back up.
The disc image stays wherever you keep it.


WHAT IS NOT QUITE RIGHT YET

Every minigame has been compared against the real game frame by frame,
and the author of this package then went through every frame by hand
(37 notes: shadows, water, black where the console draws, and single
games); what is left that a player can see:

    Mario Medley        the pool's light ripple is fainter than the
                        console's (its second ripple bends a copy of the
                        picture)
    Makin' Waves        the pool ripples at the water's corners rather
                        than at every pixel, and on purpose not as the
                        console's (see THE WATER)
    Cheep Cheep Sweep   the pond's reflection does not ripple (its ripple
                        bends a copy of the picture); its look is the
                        port's own (see THE WATER)

The ripple of those pools is a warp the card's fixed pipeline cannot do
per pixel; since 0.9.13 it is drawn at the vertices (THE WATER).  A
fragment-program path is also in this build behind --tfs, and stays off
because the Radeon's Leopard driver draws two of the three pools wrong
through it (the notes say how far it got).

Now and then the game can stop for one to two seconds and then catch
up, the music with it, when the disk is slow to answer.  Since 0.9.9 the
game's own waits are out of three of those moments -- a save no longer waits
for the one before it, the log is written in the background, and Bowser's
space and the board's ending are read ahead with the rest -- so what is
left is the disk itself holding the game.  (0.9.8 had about two or three
an hour on the reference machine; the project's notes, PLAN.md section 55,
have what 0.9.9 measured.)

With Lite mode (LITE MODE) 81 of the 82 screens measured reach 30 frames
a second on the reference machine, the seven slowest minigames among
them since 0.9.19 (Butterfly Blitz back at 30 without the nets' shadows
and with fewer fence flowers).  The one short on the last count is Manta
Rings, 29.1 there and 30.0 when measured again straight after: the
machine's edge, like Beach Volley Folly's before it (now 29.8); with Lite
off the seven are back at 27 to 29.7.
The game's own speed is the console's everywhere; only the picture is
slower where it is.  0.9.17 also draws Order Up's sparkles more cheaply,
the same pixels, for everyone.  0.9.16
brings five of those seven closer (Butterfly Blitz from about 26 to 27,
Fruits of Doom 27.4 to 28, Order Up 27.9 to 28.3, Panel Panic 28.8 to
29.4, Darts of Doom 28.8 to 29) -- the port stops re-checking every
character model's skin data every frame, writes a skinned model's new
shape without first reading the old one from memory, and wakes its second
processor's threads without making them wait on a lock -- with every
picture as 0.9.15 draws it.  0.9.15
steadies the glowing lights on the pillars of Bowser's room (Darts, Fruits
and Balloon of Doom): they sparkle sixty times a second on a console, and
shown at thirty they strobed between a big and a small ball -- each picture
now shows them between the two moments it stands for.  In a window, after
Stamp Out! had been played, Right Oar Left?'s left view could be black for
the whole race; 0.9.15 fixes that too.  It also reads the
PowerPCube launcher's settings and controls (LOADING, MOVIES, CONTROLS).
0.9.14 fixed three pictures: Right Oar Left?'s
boat lamps light the water in front of the boats again (0.9.13 had lost
that), a black flash of about a tenth of a second at the end of every
dimming of the board (the item menu, the minigame roulette, the lottery,
Bowser's and the battle's) that every version before had, and Mario
Medley's water colour; and the water has its own look (THE WATER).
0.9.13 took the character select, Boo's board, Beach
Volley Folly and two more minigames to 30 and every slower screen up, by
as much as two frames a second: the port's graphics layer was rewritten
for the G4 -- it no longer re-derives a drawing state that has not changed
since the last draw, and it hands the second processor its work in fewer,
cache-friendlier pieces.  0.9.12 took Trace Race, Koopa's board and two
more minigames to 30 and most of the slower screens up by one or two
frames a second (the port now waits only for the parts of a model the game
is about to reshape, skips texture work nobody reads, and lets the memory
protection watch small pieces of geometry too).  0.9.11 took Dungeon Duos
from about 26 frames a second to 30 and Koopa's board from about 27 to 29
(the port no longer re-reads a level's unchanging geometry every frame to
check it has not changed: the processor's memory protection tells it
instead), and a screen at the edge is now measured three times rather than
once.  0.9.10 took Trace Race and Stamp Out! from about 16 frames a second
to 28-30 (the canvases they paint are now redrawn only where they changed)
and Archaeologuess to 30 (its six-lamp rooms are lit on the graphics
card); Right Oar Left?'s boat lamps now light the water in front of the
boats, as on the console.

On a single-processor G4 the heaviest minigames fall behind the
console's speed -- Stamp Out!, which reads its own picture back to
paint with, drew about 13 frames a second on one 1 GHz processor in
0.9.8 --
and there the sound breaks up now and then while the game catches up.
A two-processor Mac does not.

The game's memory card is one card in slot A;
slot B is always empty.  A second controller works (checked with a pad on
port 1 and the keyboard standing in as player 2); three and four are
wired the same way but untested, there being one pad in the house.


LICENCE AND CREDITS

The game is the property of its rightsholders.  Nothing in this package
contains any of its data: you supply your own disc image, and the source
repository has never contained one.

The game's code comes from the mariopartyrd/marioparty4 decompilation,
compiled as is.  The MusyX audio library is Axiomatic Data Laboratories'
reimplementation (MIT).  The movie decoder's inverse DCT and Huffman
tables follow Sean Barrett's stb_image (MIT).  SDL2 is under the zlib
licence.  The menu's letters are the Terminus Font (SIL Open Font
License 1.1).  The licence texts
are in the Licences folder beside this file, with a note on the port layer
itself.

This package is built for one person's own Power Mac and is not for
redistribution.
